opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is to look past the polished version of the story. When you read someone's CV or see their famous papers, it looks like a straight line: they picked a big problem, they had a clear vision, and everything followed. But if you actually talk to these people, the real trajectory is much messier. There were projects that failed, directions they abandoned, and a lot of uncertainty about whether what they were doing mattered at all. So the first lesson is not to compare your messy middle to someone else's cleaned-up highlight reel.

The second thing is to look at *how* they chose problems rather than *which* problems they chose. The specific topic someone worked on ten years ago may not be the right topic today; the field moves really fast, especially in robotics and machine learning. What transfers is the taste. Why did they think this problem was important before everyone else did? What did they see in the data, or in the hardware, or in some failure mode, that made them commit? If you can reverse-engineer that reasoning, it's far more useful than copying the research agenda itself.

Third, many researchers I admire have a kind of consistency underneath the surface changes. Their methods might shift, from classical planning to learning, from simulation to real robots, but there's a core question they keep coming back to. For me it has been how robots can learn to do long-horizon, structured tasks in the real world. Having that north star lets you adopt new tools without feeling like you're starting over every few years.

And finally, I'd say pay attention to the people around them. Almost nobody does great work alone. The advisors, students, and collaborators, and the environment that let someone take risks, are a huge part of the story. So as a young researcher, put real thought into who you work with and what kind of community you're building, not just what papers you're writing.

r001.rationale: The response advises examining how admired researchers chose problems and reverse-engineering their reasoning, rather than copying their topics or research agendas.

r002.rationale: It says this reasoning is more useful than copying an agenda, but does not state that reflecting on it clarifies one’s understanding of one’s own research.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, partly because I was on the other side of it not that long ago.

The first thing I'd say is that you should learn from trajectories, not from snapshots. When you look at someone you admire, you tend to see them at the point where they're already successful, where their work seems coherent and inevitable. But if you actually go back and read their early papers, or hear them talk about their PhD, it's usually a lot messier than that. There are false starts, there are projects that went nowhere, there are a couple of years where they were working on something that looks completely unrelated to what they're known for now. I find that genuinely comforting, and I think young researchers should seek that out rather than just looking at the highlight reel.

The second thing is to pay attention to the questions, not just the answers. When I look at the people whose careers I admire, what's consistent isn't a particular method or a particular benchmark. Methods come and go very fast in our field. What's consistent is a taste for a certain kind of problem. For me, a lot of the people I looked up to in robotics and learning were asking some version of "how does an agent learn to do useful things in a physical world where you can't just collect infinite data?" The tools they used to attack that changed every few years, but the question was stable. So I'd encourage people to try to reverse-engineer what question someone is really after, because that's the transferable part.

Related to that, I think you should notice how people pick their battles. Good researchers I know are very deliberate about when to follow the crowd and when to step away from it. Sometimes the right move is to jump on a hot direction because that's where the tools and the community are, and you learn a lot by being in the middle of it. But at some point they each made a bet on something that wasn't obvious or fashionable at the time, and they stuck with it long enough to find out whether it was right. Learning how to time that, and how to tolerate a couple of years of being somewhat out of step, is something you can only really learn by watching others do it.

The last thing, and maybe the most important, is don't try to copy the trajectory itself. The field that your advisor or your hero came up in doesn't exist anymore. The opportunities that were open to them in 2012 or 2016 are different from what's open now. So the goal shouldn't be to retrace their steps, it should be to extract the principles, things like how they chose problems, how they dealt with being wrong, how they built collaborations, and then apply those to the landscape you're actually in. If you do it right, your trajectory should look different from theirs, and that's a sign you learned the right lesson.

r001.rationale: The response advises looking past admired researchers’ success and accomplishments to understand the questions they pursued, how they chose problems, and why they made their research bets.

r002.rationale: It recommends applying those principles to one’s own research landscape, but does not say that reflecting on researchers’ choices clarifies one’s understanding of one’s own research.

astra-6.text:
I think the most useful thing to learn is how they made decisions, not just which topics they worked on. When you look at someone’s career in hindsight, it can seem like a very clear sequence: they did this project, then that led to the next big idea. But at the time, they probably had a lot of uncertainty, and there were things that didn’t work that you don’t see in the final papers.

So I would ask: What were they seeing that made a problem worth pursuing? When did they decide to keep pushing, and when did they change direction? Those are lessons you can apply even if you work on a completely different topic.

And I think it helps to look at several people you admire, because there isn’t one trajectory you’re supposed to follow. The goal is to develop your own judgment—to understand what you find important and where you can contribute—rather than try to reproduce somebody else’s career.

r001.rationale: It says to focus on how admired researchers made decisions and what made a problem worth pursuing, rather than simply listing the topics or projects they worked on.

r002.rationale: It connects examining those choices to developing one’s own judgment and understanding what one finds important and where one can contribute.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most useful thing to learn is how they made decisions, rather than just which topics they worked on. When you look at someone’s career retrospectively, it can seem like a very clear trajectory. But at each point, they probably had uncertainty, ideas that didn’t work, and opportunities they couldn’t have anticipated.

So I would ask: What were they trying to understand? Why did they stick with a problem, or decide to move on? How did they change their mind? Those are things you can learn from without trying to reproduce their career. The field changes, and your own strengths and interests will be different. You want to develop your own judgment, not just inherit someone else’s choice of problems.
